title: Keyset Pagination vs Deep OFFSET: Eliminating O(N) Query Degradation
realWorldScenario: A public product listing API allows customers to paginate through 1,000,000 products. Page 1 (`OFFSET 0 LIMIT 20`) loads in 1ms. Page 20,000 (`OFFSET 400000 LIMIT 20`) takes 8.5 seconds and causes severe database disk reads.
questionStatement: Explain why SQL `OFFSET` scales with $O(N)$ time complexity. Write an optimized keyset pagination query (seek method) using a composite cursor `(created_at, id)` that executes in $O(1)$ constant time regardless of page depth, and demonstrate the required composite B-tree index.
starterCode:
-- Optimized keyset pagination query (Page 2+ using composite cursor)
-- Cursor from previous page: last_created_at = '2026-01-03', last_id = 3
SELECT 
    id,
    name,
    price,
    created_at
FROM products
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-01-03', 3)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
expectedConcepts: OFFSET scanning and discarding N rows in memory/disk
Linear O(N) degradation of deep OFFSET queries
O(log N) B-tree seek followed by O(LIMIT) scan
Composite index matching sort order: (created_at DESC, id DESC)
hints: Why does OFFSET 400000 force Postgres to read 400,020 rows?
Tuple comparisons like (col1, col2) < (val1, val2) are directly supported by B-tree indexes.
Why include the primary key id in the tie-breaker?

testCases.description: Verify keyset pagination returns next batch after cursor
testCases.setupSql:
CREATE TABLE products (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(50), price NUMERIC, created_at VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO products VALUES (1, 'Laptop', 1000, '2026-01-01'), (2, 'Phone', 800, '2026-01-02'), (3, 'Tablet', 500, '2026-01-03');
testCases.expectedOutputSql: SELECT id, name, price, created_at FROM products WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-01-03', 3) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;
